subject: Efficient way to break up permutation test

messages.author: 2c7106159c8e6d5b
messages.subject: Efficient way to break up permutation test
parts:
With DO animals, n > 1000, 20 phenotypes, and especially, separate permutations for autosomes and X chromosome (permXsp=T), estimating empirical thresholds takes a very long time. I'm farming out the permutations to a computing cluster with many cores, but that cluster has per-job time restrictions. 

So, I'm going to break the job up into parts and concatenate the permutation results after the fact. I'd like to know if scan1perms is written such that it will make a difference in processing time if I break up the job by (a) permuting each phenotype separately, or (b) permuting all phenotypes together, but with a relatively small number of permutation per job. E.g., with option (b) there would be some (perhaps minimal) speed-up if the same permutation of the data were applied to all 20 phenotypes.

A third option would be to split the job into autosomes (for which permutations maxLODs are estimated relatively quickly) and the X-chromosome (much slower).

Thanks.

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Efficient way to break up permutation test
parts:
If you’re using an additive allele model (that is, with allele dosages rather than genotypes), the X chromosome and autosomes in the DO will both have 7 degrees of freedom, and so you shouldn’t need to use separate thresholds for the autosomes and the X chromosome. (If you use permXsp=TRUE, do you get pretty similar thresholds for both?) Getting X-chr-specific thresholds should take about twice as long. The time to get a bunch more replicates on the X chromosome should be able the same as the time devoted to the autosomes.

Regarding splitting up, it may be somewhat faster to work with one phenotype at a time, but I don’t think it will make much difference; with a linear mixed model we do the analysis with one phenotype at a time anyway. If you do the multiple phenotypes together and split the permutations into groups, the results will maintain the correlations among phenotypes, which can be useful for some purposes (such as to adjust for the consideration of multiple phenotypes.

In summary I don’t think it will matter and you should just focus on what’s most convenient code-wise. For me, that’d be to split the total permutations into smaller batches, one batch per computer.

karl

Then I'll start batches for the second part of that comparison, using the same threshold for autosomes and X. 

And yes, X chromosome thresholds do seem to take a little less than twice as long to run. 

Quick follow-up: I'm confused by the dimensions of $X output from scan1. One permutation for p traits results in a 19 x p matrix of maximum LOD scores. 19 autosomes?

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Efficient way to break up permutation test
parts:
On 4/28/19 8:12 PM, David Katz wrote:
Quick follow-up: I'm confused by the dimensions of $X output from scan1. One permutation for p traits results in a 19 x p matrix of maximum LOD scores. 19 autosomes?

With perm_Xsp=TRUE, the output of scan1perm() will be a list with two components named "A" and "X".
Each should be a matrix with rows being permutation replicates and columns being phenotypes.
The values in the A matrix are the maximum LOD score across all autosomes for that trait in that replicate. The values for the X matrix are the maximum LOD score across the X chromosome for that trait in that replicate.

The separate maxima for the 19 autosomes wouldn't be retained anywhere.

karl

messages.author: 2c7106159c8e6d5b
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Efficient way to break up permutation test
parts:
Yes, the output is strange. I spent some time looking over scan1perm on github but couldn't see a problem.

The data for this sample is far too large to share over email. With 'apr' the allele probabilities and 'cr' the cross2 object, these are the data objects for analysis.
probs <- apr # allele probabilities
map <- cr$gmap # 'cr' is the cross file
pheno <- cr$pheno
pheno_model <- data.frame(cr$pheno[,1:20])
colnames(pheno_model)<-paste0("PC", 1:20)
sex = (cr$covar$Sex=="M")*1
covs_model <- data.frame(Sex = sex, Age=as.numeric(cr$covar$AgeSac))
rownames(covs_model)<- rownames(cr$covar)
 K <- readRDS(file.path(fullpath, "data/K_loco.rds")) # leave-one-chromosome out kinship matrices

Here is the call to the scan1perm function for a single permutation
perms <- 1
operm <- scan1perm(genoprobs = probs, pheno = pheno_model, 
                      kinship = K, addcovar = covs_model,
                      model = "normal", n_perm = perms, 
                      perm_Xsp = T, 
                      chr_lengths = chr_lengths(map), cores=1)

The rdata output is attached.

David

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Efficient way to break up permutation test
parts:
Here, the results for the autosomes the matrix is 1 x 20 because there
is one permutation replicate and 20 phenotypes.
For the X chromosome, the result is 19 x 20, because there are 19
permutation replicates and 20 phenotypes.

With perm_Xsp=TRUE, we do more replicates for the X chromosome than for
the autosomes, because we are trying to estimate a quantile much farther
out in the tail. If L_A is the length of the autosomes and L_X is the
length of the X chromosome, we use n x L_A / L_X permutations for the X
chromosome.

karl
